items.stem: What is the time complexity of reading the element at a known index in an array?

options.text: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)

readingJson.reason: Reading an element at a known index in an array is a constant‑time operation because the memory address of the element can be computed directly from the base address and the index. Therefore the time complexity is O(1).

items.stem: Which transport protocol retransmits lost segments so that data arrives complete and in order?

options.text: TCP
UDP
ICMP
ARP

readingJson.reason: TCP is a transport protocol that provides reliable, ordered delivery by retransmitting lost segments.

TCP is a connection-oriented protocol that uses acknowledgments and retransmission to ensure reliable data transfer, guaranteeing that lost segments are resent and data arrives in order. In contrast, UDP does not provide such mechanisms, and ICMP and ARP serve different functions without handling data retransmission.

items.stem: Which data structure removes elements in first in, first out order?

options.text: Stack
Queue
Binary search tree
Hash table

readingJson.reason: A queue is a linear structure that follows the first‑in, first‑out (FIFO) order when removing elements. A stack uses LIFO, binary search trees and hash tables do not enforce a FIFO removal order.

A queue is defined by the first-in, first-out (FIFO) principle, where elements are removed in the same order they were added. A stack uses last-in, first-out order, while binary search trees and hash tables have no inherent FIFO removal behavior.

items.stem: In big-O notation, what does O(n) say about an algorithm?

options.text: It always takes exactly n steps to finish
Its running time grows at most linearly with the input size
It uses n bytes of memory whatever the input
It is faster than every O(log n) algorithm

readingJson.reason: Big-O notation describes an asymptotic upper bound, so O(n) means the algorithm's running time grows no faster than a constant multiple of the input size n. Options A and C incorrectly imply exact values, and D is wrong because asymptotic bounds ignore constant factors and lower-order terms that determine actual speed for any given input.

O(n) indicates that the algorithm's running time grows at most linearly as the input size increases, not that it takes exactly n steps. It does not describe memory usage and is not generally faster than algorithms with lower growth rates like O(log n).

O(n) describes an upper bound on the running time that grows proportionally to the input size, meaning the time does not exceed a constant multiple of n for sufficiently large inputs. It does not guarantee exact step counts, memory usage, or comparisons to other complexities.

items.stem: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, and no preemption are three of the four conditions required for deadlock. What is the fourth?

options.text: Round-robin scheduling
Virtual memory
Circular wait
Context switching

readingJson.reason: The fourth necessary condition for deadlock is circular wait, where each process holds resources needed by another process in a chain. Without circular wait, a deadlock cannot occur even if the other three conditions are satisfied.

The four Coffman conditions required for deadlock are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Round-robin scheduling, virtual memory, and context switching are unrelated operating system concepts and not conditions for deadlock.

items.stem: Which layer of the TCP/IP model does HTTP belong to?

options.text: Transport
Presentation
Application
Internet

readingJson.reason: HTTP is an application layer protocol in the TCP/IP model, used for web communication. It operates on top of the transport layer, which provides end-to-end communication services.

HTTP is an application-layer protocol in the TCP/IP model because it defines the rules for communication between web clients and servers. The TCP/IP model does not include a Presentation layer, and HTTP does not perform transport or internet-layer functions like segmenting traffic or routing packets.

HTTP is an application-layer protocol in the TCP/IP model, providing the rules for client-server communication over the web. The TCP/IP model does not include a Presentation layer, the Transport layer handles end-to-end delivery with protocols like TCP, and the Internet layer handles addressing and routing with IP.

items.stem: What does a primary key guarantee about a relational table?

options.text: Every column in the table holds a number
Rows are returned in the order they were inserted
The table is joined to exactly one other table
Every row can be identified by a value that is unique and not null

readingJson.reason: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table and cannot contain null values. This guarantees that every row can be referenced by a unique, non‑null identifier.

A primary key is defined by the relational model as a column or combination of columns that uniquely identifies each row and cannot contain null values. The other options describe unrelated or incorrect properties: columns may be any data type, tables have no inherent row order, and primary keys impose no requirements on how many tables a table may be joined with.

A primary key ensures each row is uniquely identifiable by a value or combination of values that cannot be null, which is the core guarantee of entity integrity in the relational model. None of the other options describe properties enforced by a primary key, as tables may contain various data types, have no inherent row order, and may be joined to any number of other tables.

items.stem: What does a compiler do with a source program?

options.text: Translates it into another language, usually machine code, before it runs
Runs it one statement at a time without translating it
Reformats it to match the project style guide
Removes unused files from the project directory

readingJson.reason: A compiler translates source code into another language, usually machine code, before the program runs, whereas an interpreter executes statements one at a time without translating them first.

A compiler translates source code written in a high-level programming language into another language, typically machine code or assembly, before the program executes. This distinguishes it from an interpreter, which runs code one statement at a time during runtime without producing a separate translated program beforehand.

A compiler translates the entire source program into another language—typically machine code or bytecode—before execution begins, producing an output file that can be run independently. This is fundamentally different from an interpreter, which processes and executes statements one at a time without producing a separate translated program first.

items.stem: What is the main job of the Domain Name System?

options.text: Handing out IP addresses to devices joining a network
Choosing a route for packets travelling between networks
Encrypting the traffic between a browser and a web server
Translating domain names into IP addresses

readingJson.reason: The Domain Name System’s primary purpose is to resolve human‑friendly domain names into the numeric IP addresses that computers use to communicate. Although DNS can be involved in other tasks such as load balancing, its core function is name‑to‑address translation.

The Domain Name System primarily translates human-readable domain names into machine-readable IP addresses, enabling users to reach websites without memorizing numerical addresses. The other options describe separate technologies—DHCP, routing protocols, and TLS encryption—each with a different core purpose.

items.stem: Why does a processor have a cache?

options.text: To keep files after the machine is switched off
To keep recently used data closer to the processor than main memory is
To add more cores to the processor
To translate assembly language into machine code

readingJson.reason: A cache provides a small, fast memory near the CPU that stores recently accessed data and instructions, reducing the time the processor spends waiting for main memory. This improves overall performance by minimizing memory access latency.

Cache memory stores frequently or recently accessed data in fast memory physically closer to the processor than main memory, which reduces access latency. The other options incorrectly describe non-volatile storage, processor multicore architecture, and assembly translation.

items.stem: How many bytes are there in one kilobyte?

readingJson.reason: In the SI standard a kilobyte equals 1000 bytes, but in computing the traditional definition treats a kilobyte as 1024 bytes. Since the question is from a computer‑science perspective, the conventional answer is 1024.

In traditional computer science usage, one kilobyte equals 1024 bytes (2^10), though a competent reader could also select 1000 based on the SI definition of the SI prefix 'kilo-' and modern standards like IEC 80000-13 which reserve 1024 for the kibibyte.
